At a glance worst case anywhere in Puget Sound, Admiralty, the Strait and the northern waters,

Each tile is the highest value any one of these zones carries for that period, and names the zone it came from — a single number for two hundred miles of water would be either the calmest place you are not, or an average of places with nothing to do with each other. Coastal and offshore are reported separately below each tile rather than folded in: they are the roughest water in the document by a wide margin, and an unqualified worst case would read "eighteen feet" off a zone 150 NM out every day of the year. These are FORECAST values from the zone bulletins, not observations.

Times follow a fixed UTC schedule, so they shift by an hour when daylight saving ends.

NWS Seattle Area Forecast Discussion source

Issued Sat 26 Sep 08:25 PDT 15:25Z 1 h 38 m ago current

SYNOPSIS

Weather settling down today with upper level trough to the east, surface high pressure over the area and split flow aloft developing off the coast. Little change in the pattern tonight and Sunday. Flow aloft consolidating off the coast Sunday night but next system not reaching the area until Tuesday. Much weaker system most likely will fall apart before it gets to Western Washington Thursday. Upper level ridge building Friday with thermally induced surface trough developing along the Oregon coast.

SHORT TERM — TODAY THROUGH MONDAY

No major updates have been made this morning. See below for an updated aviation section.

Dry weekend in store for Western Washington. Upper level trough east of the area early this morning. Surface high pressure building today. Split flow aloft developing off the coast today as well. Little change in the pattern tonight and Sunday. Patchy fog developing this morning will dissipate before late morning. A little more fog coverage Sunday morning as the air mass continues to calm down. Highs today and Sunday even with some sunshine a little below normal, lower to mid 60s. Lows tonight in the 40s and lower 50s.

Pattern changes beginning Sunday night with the flow aloft becoming consolidated off the coast. Next system well to the northwest, near Haida Gwaii. Mostly clear skies allowing temperatures to drop into the upper 30s and 40s. The forecast low of 46 at Seattle-Tacoma airport would be the coldest low since 45 degrees on May 30th.

Increasing middle and high level clouds Monday as the next weather system continues to move southeast down the British Columbia coast. Chance of rain along the north coast by late in the afternoon. Highs again in the lower to mid 60s. Felton

LONG TERM — MONDAY NIGHT THROUGH FRIDAY

Models in good agreement with rain out ahead of the system over the northern portion of the area Monday night. Slow moving front dragging through Western Washington Tuesday into Tuesday night. Not much cool air behind the front with minimal post frontal shower activity Wednesday.

Inconsistency in the solutions increasing Wednesday night through Thursday night. Operational runs are dry but enough ensemble solutions indicating light precipitation to keep slight chance pops in the forecast. Confidence in this scenario not very high. Will not be surprised if the pops fall out of the forecast in the next few runs.

ECMWF has strong upper level ridge building Friday with thermally induced surface trough developing along the Oregon coast. GFS has this scenario as well but is 24 hours behind the ECMWF. For now the general idea is dry and warmer heading into next weekend. Felton

AVIATION

Northwesterly flow aloft this morning and this afternoon as an upper level ridge builds over the coastal waters. This will turn more zonal this evening as split flow develops between this low and a developing trough off the OR waters. Surface winds south to southwesterly this morning before turning more north to northeasterly this afternoon. Speeds generally 4-8 kts this morning before increasing to 8-12 kts this afternoon. Wind speeds expected to ease tonight back into that initial 4-8 kts range.

Most locations still seeing VFR conditions this early morning although some isolated MVFR to IFR conditions are present. As winds continue to ease this morning, cigs expected to lower due to abundant low-level moisture with widespread MVFR/IFR conditions expected by 12Z this morning. Cigs expected to lift and return to VFR in the usual 18-20Z time frame and persist for the remainder of the TAF period.

KSEA...VFR conditions in place with FEW-SCT clouds around 2000 ft. VFR still expected around 18Z with skies clearing throughout the day thanks to building upper level ridge. Southerly surface winds turning northerly after 18Z with speeds increasing to 8-12 kts.

33/18

MARINE

Weak high pressure and winds turning light offshore today. On Sunday, an approaching frontal system will dissipate over the offshore waters. A stronger frontal system will reach WA Monday night and Tuesday with increasing south winds. Additional headlines may be needed for this time frame should forecast remain consistent.

Seas generally 5-7 feet and will continue to ease this morning until reaching 3-5 ft by noon today. Wave heights rebound this evening slightly this evening to 4-6 ft before reaching 7-9 ft Sunday and into Monday. With frontal passage expected Tuesday, seas may rise to 9-11 ft and may need headlines.

33/18

SEW WATCHES/WARNINGS/ADVISORIES

Verbatim automatic captions from YouTube, unedited.

GOES-West — GeoColor

Two scales: the U.S. Pacific Coast for systems still offshore, and the NWS Seattle county warning area for what is overhead. GeoColor is day true colour, night multispectral IR. Both loops start when you scroll to them and drop back to their still when you scroll away — a 1000 × 1000 animation expands to hundreds of megabytes of decoded frames, so releasing the ones you are not looking at is what keeps that bounded.

Radar

ASCAT coastal winds — outer coast source

12.5 km resolution resolves the outer coast but not Puget Sound or, marginally, the Strait — a geometry limit, not a data problem. Read these for the PZZ150/PZZ170 stretch only.
Each file is a single satellite swath and the source zone spans the whole US West Coast, so the plotted latitude range is read off each image's own axis and passes that miss 48.0°N are discarded — many show California. Of 15 recent passes across 3 days, 4 cover these waters and 7 did not.

Forecast maps — wind and fog from HRRR, RRFS, REFS and UW WRF-ARW

HRRR High-Resolution Rapid Refresh

Run by
NOAA/NCEP, operational
Type
WRF-ARW core, convection-allowing
Grid
3 km, CONUS
Cycles
Hourly to 18 h; 00/06/12/18Z out to 48 h
Strategy
Assimilates radar and refreshes every hour, so the near term is re-anchored on what is actually happening

Sharpest short-range detail here, and the freshest — a new run every hour.

Most cycles reach only 18 h, so it drops out of the later steps. Slated to be replaced by RRFS.

RRFS Rapid Refresh Forecast System

Run by
NOAA/NCEP — v1.0 pre-production, not yet general availability
Type
FV3 core, convection-allowing
Grid
3 km, CONUS
Cycles
Hourly to 18 h; 00/06/12/18Z out to 84 h
Strategy
HRRR's designated successor on NOAA's newer dynamical core

Much the longest reach on this page — 84 h against HRRR's 48 h — so it alone covers a multi-day plan.

Pre-production: availability, timing and quality can change without notice, and its extended run completes ~8.5 h after cycle time, so it is always the older of the two here.

REFS Rapid Refresh Ensemble Forecast System

Run by
NOAA/NCEP — built from RRFS, so pre-production with it
Type
Ensemble: the current and 6 h older RRFS runs plus the RRFS ensemble members, combined into products
Grid
3 km, CONUS
Cycles
00/06/12/18Z, hourly out to 60 h
Strategy
Not one forecast but how much the forecasts disagree

The only thing on this page that says how SURE the wind forecast is: spread shows where the members disagree, and the chance maps put a number on reaching 20 or 35 kt — and on fog under 1 mi or ½ mi, and on lightning.

No gust product at all. Its chances are neighbourhood probabilities — wind somewhere near a point, not at it — and its mean direction is withheld wherever the members disagree on one.

UW WRF-ARW University of Washington real-time

Run by
UW Atmospheric Sciences — their site carries the full product set, other fields and domains
Type
WRF-ARW, nested to a local domain
Grid
1.33 km — by far the finest here
Reach
0–72 h, hourly, on two fixed domains that this page matches exactly
Strategy
Resolve the terrain the coarser models smooth away — the gaps, channels and passes that actually steer wind here

The only model on this page that resolves the terrain channelling through the Strait, Admiralty and the gaps.

Pre-rendered images, not data: UW's own projection and barbs, so it will not line up pixel for pixel. Its URL carries no cycle at all, so the run time has to be read off the frame itself.

10 m wind — colour fill on the water is speed, grey streamlines are direction, and magenta contours are mean sea level pressure at 1 hPa, the same interval the UW frames use. Pick any run in any of the four panes; all four are driven by one control and matched on valid time, not lead, so runs on different cycles line up correctly. It opens on HRRR (left) against RRFS (right) for the northern waters (top) and Puget Sound (bottom), all on the freshest hourly runs — but any pane can be switched to an extended run, the other domain, or UW WRF. RRFS forecasts 84 h against HRRR's 48 h, so later steps may carry only one. Blink alternates each row's two panes in place — differences read far more clearly as movement than side by side.
Hover over a map, or tap it, for the numbers at that point — wind, gust and direction on HRRR and RRFS, with HRRR's visibility when it is under 5 mi and its lightning when there is any; on REFS the mean, spread, every wind chance, and the chance of fog and lightning whenever REFS gives them any. A tap pins the point, so stepping through time with one spot pinned shows the forecast there hour by hour. UW panes are UW's own images with no values behind them.
Gust panes show each model's surface gust on the same scale as the wind, so a wind pane and its gust pane read colour for colour. REFS is NOAA's high-resolution ensemble: its mean is on the wind scale too, while its spread (how far the members disagree) and its chance maps have keys of their own in the pane. The chances are neighbourhood probabilities — the chance of that wind somewhere near each point — which is why they spread out beside a gap jet rather than tracing it. Where the members disagree on direction, the REFS maps draw no streamlines and the readout gives no bearing: a gap in the arrows is the ensemble saying it does not know which way the wind will blow there, often across a wind shift.
HRRR run to run uses the fact that HRRR starts a new run every hour, so its last six runs all forecast the next dozen hours. Spread is how far they disagree at each point; trend is the newest run minus the ones before it — red where each new run comes in windier, blue where it is backing off, white inside a knot either way. A forecast that keeps moving is one to hold loosely, and which way it is moving is often the more useful half. The readout lists every run's value at the point, oldest first.
Fog. Fog in the control bar sets all four panes at once: HRRR's visibility beside REFS's chance of visibility under 1 mi, northern waters above Puget Sound, on the extended HRRR run so the pair reaches the next morning; Wind puts them back. HRRR's visibility colours the water only under 5 mi, darkest in the thickest fog. REFS's chances — under 1 mi and under ½ mi — are neighbourhood chances like its wind ones. Model fog is the least reliable thing on these maps: a marine layer a few hundred feet thick is close to what a 3 km model can resolve, so treat the chance maps as the better guide and the observations as the final word. RRFS publishes visibility only in a form this page cannot fetch cheaply, so it has none.
Lightning is not drawn as a map — over these waters it comes a few days a year, and a lightning pane would be blank the rest. It is in the readout instead: tap any HRRR or REFS pane and HRRR's threat (trace, possible, likely, strong — words, because the index is not a probability) and REFS's chance appear whenever there is any.
One scale across all three models. The HRRR and RRFS panels are rendered on UW's own wind palette, sampled from the colour bar of a real UW frame, and on the measured extents of UW's two 1.33 km domains — so a colour means the same speed over the same ground in every pane, UW's included. Note the palette is UW's, not a designed ramp: it runs pale blue → pale green → tan → yellow → pink → grey → green → cyan → blue → red, turning back toward cool colours above 30 kt. Each printed number marks the middle of its band, as on UW's own bar — “10” means 7.5–12.5 kt — so small craft (21 kt) and gale (34 kt) fall inside bands rather than on colour changes. White is under 2.5 kt, not missing data, and red is over 47.5. UW still draws its own frames in its own projection with barbs instead of streamlines, so fine detail will not line up pixel for pixel.

Open the dedicated comparison page → — the same runs with nothing else on the page, so the panes get the whole window. Choose two panes and they sit side by side at full height on a desktop and stack full width on a phone; choose four and they go two-up, still on one screen. Every pane carries its own time control, so you can step through without scrolling back up.

Lightning

Six independent ways to notice lightning, for each of the three areas a passage here crosses. Each area counts anything within 10 nm of its water — about how far a strike reaches from a storm — so convection over the Cascade and Olympic crests does not set it off. The verdict rests on the most authoritative source with something to say, and no source can lower another.

covered, nothingtrace possible · NWS thunderstorms likelystrong does not reach — not the same as no model steps back to its older, longer run

NWS gridpoint: the official gridded forecast at 18 points on the water — two to six per marine zone, Hood Canal and the South Sound past the Narrows included — the worst of an area's points each hour, with the forecaster's coverage word — a slight chance of thunderstorms is already a watch; likely or heavier, an alert. NWS zone forecast: the marine zone bulletin's periods whose text mentions thunderstorms. HRRR: its lightning threat anywhere in reach, from the freshest run covering each hour (18 h hourly, 48 h extended) — an index, not a probability, so it is banded in words. RRFS: the same index as each hour's maximum, likewise freshest run first (18 h hourly, 84 h extended). A tick marks where either model steps back from its hourly run to the older extended one — a change there may be the run, not the weather. REFS: the ensemble's chance of any lightning nearby — under 10% is a trace, 10% a watch, 40% likely. Past hours fade as you read; hover a cell for what that source says.

No mention of thunderstorms or lightning in the NWS Seattle forecast discussion.

Offshore

A different product from a different office: the Ocean Prediction Center's Offshore Waters Forecast, issued on its own schedule and with its own synopsis below. Wind is written as a range there (“W to NW”) and sometimes only as a ceiling (“less than 10 kt”), which is why some cells carry a maximum with no minimum.

PZZ898 Offshore synopsis — Washington and Oregon waters source
Issued Sat 26 Sep 07:34 PDT 14:34Z 2 h 29 m ago Expires Sat 26 Sep 21:15 PDT current

A low pressure trough will extend N to the Washington coast today before weakening tonight into Sun night. A cold front will approach the area from the W today and weaken near the outer waters tonight, then dissipate Sun. High pressure will again build E across the waters later Sun and Sun night. The ridge of high pressure will slide S and SE ahead of yet another approaching cold front Mon. The front will enter the NW portions late Mon, then stall across the Washington waters Mon night. The front will slowly lift N as a warm front Tue, and clear N of the area Tue night. Yet another cold front will approach and move SE across the NW waters Tue night, then move slowly across the regional waters Wed into Wed night.

Experimental — Pressure Gradient Axes

Burch's empirical rule, computed from live barometers. The geostrophic trace is the frictionless upper bound, shown for context — real surface wind runs below it.

Pressure and wind at each station on this axis, against the models. Black is the station's own record over the last 24 h; solid colour is the latest hourly run of each model, dashed is its extended run. Violet is the REFS ensemble mean, with a shaded band of ± its spread on the wind row — narrow where the members agree, wide where they do not. The faint dotted line above each wind trace is its gust — the station's measured gust, or the model's diagnosed surface gust (REFS has none). Behind the HRRR line, fainter orange lines are HRRR's last six runs, the oldest faintest: where they fan out the model has been changing its mind, and if each is above the last the forecast is ramping up. The readout lists their values oldest first. All are read from the model grid cell containing the station. Where a coloured line sits left of “now” it is that run's own early leads, so the gap between it and the black line is how the model has been doing so far. Move the pointer across a chart — or tap it on a phone — to read every trace at that hour at once, rather than having to land on a line.

Tidal Currents CO-OPS

Harmonic predictions are reliable for tidal timing, but carry no wind or river effects the way SSCOFS's dynamical forecast does — worth checking both, especially in stormy conditions.

Stations run south to north. Columns are the nth event of that station's day — they carry no fixed event type, because stations are phase-shifted from one another. Each cell states its own event. Depth of the near-surface bin differs per station and is shown with the station.

Current forecast maps — SSCOFS, rendered here

Near-surface currents from the surface sigma layer (siglay 0, ~1.6% depth), on the same two boxes as the wind panels — so a current frame and a wind frame of the same hour cover identical ground — but named for what they hold when you are reading current: the northern box runs Neah Bay to Bellingham, the southern is Puget Sound with Admiralty. Run init Sat 26 Sep 2026 02:00 PDT / 2026-09-26 09:00 UTC. Peak in this run: 9.4 kt.
Colour is speed, dark lines are direction. This is not the wind scale — currents run an order of magnitude slower, so the bands are 0.5–8 kt, not 2.5–52.5. Blank water means outside the model's own mesh, not slack.
Hover anywhere on a panel to read the modelled speed at that spot in knots. The readout samples a ~600 m cell, so in the narrowest passes — Deception, The Narrows, Admiralty — it can sit a little under a true point value where the shear is steep. Use the harmonic table above for the number at a specific station.
